docs.title: Batch Processing
docs.text:
Batch processing is one of the most common patterns one faces when dealing with data. There is typically a big dataset to be processed made of several splits (subfolders). These splits can be often processed independently as separate tasks, which helps reducing size and wall time of the job. Pipelines can be set up in this way when processing data in batches with sdag:

from pathlib import Path

from sdag import Artifact, pipeline, script


@pipeline
def process_in_batches(input_path: str, base_output: str):
    for split in ["split1", "split2", "split3"]:
        output_path = Path(base_output) / split
        t = process_split(
            input_path=input_path, split=split, output_path=output_path
        )
        t.name = f"process-{split}"


@process_in_batches.task(script, cache="io")
def process_split(input_path: Path, split: str, output_path: Artifact[Path]):
    print(
        f"processing '{split}' in '{input_path}' and saving"
        f" it to {output_path}"
    )

In this way, splits are processed independently from each other. These tasks get custom names for easier traceability in the logs and separate caches. If some splits fail, you can use sdag retry to restart only the failed ones. If new splits are added to the dataset, the other ones got cached so they won't be processed again during subsequent runs. You can run this example through:

sdag run process_in_batches --local --input-path=input --base-output=output

docs.title: Job Arrays
docs.text:
The approach shown in the previous section is very flexible. However, there is a drawback. If the number of splits is too high, many tiny jobs will be created, thus putting significant pressure on the Slurm queuing system. For this reason, only on Slurm it is possible to leverage each to orchestrate batch processing with job arrays:

from sdag import each, pipeline, script


@pipeline
def job_array():
    shards = ["a", "b", "c"]
    t = process_shards(items=each(shards))
    gather(items=t)


@job_array.task(script, njobs=2)
def process_shards(items: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    return items


@job_array.task(script, cmd="bash")
def gather(items: list[list[str]]) -> None:
    # items = [["a", "b"], ["c"]]
    print(f"collected items: {items}")

shards here can also be the output of a task but it must always be a list. Shards are equally split into an array of two jobs (the number of jobs is automatically decreased if the number of items is lower than that). If retries are enabled, only failed jobs are resubmitted. Other than that, an array mostly behaves like a single task and its cache is also unique. This is in contrast with the previous example, where each split had its own cache. This example only runs on Slurm:

sdag run job_array

Warning

Arrays are mostly treated as single jobs by Slurm and they must be submitted all at once. Therefore, sdag will submit the whole array and limit the number of running jobs to the value selected by the user. This means the total number of running jobs could be higher than the maximum one if other tasks are running. This is usually not an issue as the number of array jobs typically dominates the total number of jobs in a pipeline.

docs.title: Handling Multiple Runs of the Same Pipeline
docs.text:
You rarely need multiple concurrent runs of the same pipeline. In fact, calling the same pipeline multiple times with different arguments typically involves writing a bash script that must be maintained, which is exactly what sdag tries to avoid. A better approach would be to define an outer pipeline that calls the inner pipelines multiple times.

Nevertheless, it's still possible to run, kill, and restart multiple runs of the same pipeline. The maximum number of pipelines that can be handled at the same time can be specified by the max-concurrent-runs configuration in the pyproject.toml. Once that number is reached, the oldest runs are deleted to make room for the new ones. When compiled, each JSON file is assigned a unique hash that is then used to uniquely identify that run. The same hash is also periodically printed in the scheduler logs:

2026-09-21T19:06:35Z INFO  core::engine::summary] Pipeline 'hello_world' with hash '121a42773f77941c' - Summary:

You can use sdag list <pipeline-name> to view hashes and timestamps of all the available runs. sdag restart, sdag retry, and sdag kill accept an optional --hash argument to restart or kill specific runs. By default, the target becomes the most recent one.

docs.title: Detaching Commands
docs.text:
On public supercomputers, jobs running on login nodes usually have limited resources and wall time. The Rust scheduler of sdag is intentionally lightweight so it can typically survive many hours on login nodes without being killed. If the SSH connection goes down, sdag restart can be used to safely restart the scheduler and pick the execution from where it left off.

Nevertheless, for long workflows across large graphs it may be better to just submit the scheduler as a Slurm job on a compute node. This can be achieved by adding the --detach option to the CLI command. For example:

sdag run <pipeline-name> --detach

will compile and start the scheduler as a separate Slurm job. By default, these commands are executed on 1 CPU (nodes = 1, tasks-per-node = 1, and cpus-per-task = 1) and inherit account, partition, and qos from pyproject.toml/.sdag.toml config files. stdout and stderr are written in a ./logs/sdag folder. The default behavior can be modified through the [tool.sdag.detach] options in the pyproject.toml. Check out the Configuration section for details.

When the detached scheduler starts, you can use:

sdag status <pipeline-name>

to print the status table of the last checkpoint without checking the scheduler logs manually.

docs.title: Entrypoint Customization
docs.text:
So far, sdag-execute has always been used to run tasks. There are a few reasons to modify the task entrypoint, one of them being logging customization. sdag configures its own logger when running tasks. By default, everything is logged to stderr so that it can be easily captured by Slurm and written in the error file. To modify logging and in general to wrap the task call with some custom logic, you need to create an entrypoint for the sdag task execution. Create an entrypoint.py module and paste the following code:

entrypoint.py
from sdag import sdag_execute


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sdag_execute(configure_logger=False)

It is now possible to create a submit.sh file with a call to this module:

submit.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<account-name>
#SBATCH --partition=<partition-name>
#SBATCH --qos=<qos-name>
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --tasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=00:00:30

python path/to/entrypoint.py

In this way, entrypoint.py becomes the entry point of every task and the call can be wrapped in custom logic. The configure_logger option can be set to False to disable the default logging configuration.

docs.title: Structuring Larger Projects
docs.text:
When working with larger projects made of many pipelines, it is convenient to set the directory sdag searches pipelines into explicitly. Both flat and src layouts are supported. The only important point is to add __init__.py files to all subfolders in the tree to let sdag treat them as regular, importable packages.

This example takes advantage of the hello.py module created in the first example:

hello.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def hello_world():
    say_hello(name="sdag")


@hello_world.task(script)
def say_hello(name: str):
    print(f"hello from {name}")

docs.title: Flat layout
docs.text:
Create a <package-name>/workflows directory and an empty __init__.py module inside it. Now, copy the hello.py module from the previous example in the workflows/ folder. Finally, copy the following snippet inside the pyproject.toml file:

pyproject.toml
[tool.sdag]
dagdir = "<package-name>/workflows"

Your project tree should look like this:

flat layout
<package-name>
├── pyproject.toml
└── <package-name>
    ├── __init__.py
    └── workflows
        ├── __init__.py    <- Don't forget to add this
        └── hello.py       <- hello_world pipeline

docs.title: src layout
docs.text:
Create a src/<package-name>/workflows directory and an empty __init__.py module inside it. Now copy the hello.py module from the previous example in the workflows/ folder. Finally, copy the following snippet inside the pyproject.toml file:

pyproject.toml
[tool.sdag]
dagdir = "src/<package-name>/workflows"

Your project tree should look like this:

src layout
<package-name>
├── pyproject.toml
└── src
    └── <package-name>
        ├── __init__.py
        └── workflows
            ├── __init__.py    <- Don't forget to add this
            └── hello.py       <- hello_world pipeline

docs.title: Importing and running pipelines
docs.text:
Now that everything is set up, you can list the available pipelines:

sdag list

you should see the hello_world pipeline available. You can run the pipeline through:

sdag run hello_world --local

If you don't like to specify --local every time, you can add it to the pyproject.toml:

pyproject.toml
[tool.sdag]
dagdir = "<flat-or-src-layout>/workflows"
local = true

So that every task will be executed locally with bash.

docs.title: Nested Calls
docs.text:
Add the following pipeline to a new module in the main project directory:

nested.py
from pathlib import Path

from sdag import Artifact, pipeline, script, task


@pipeline
def outer_pipeline():
    t = inner_pipeline()
    global_task(path=t.artifacts["global_task"]["path"])


@pipeline
def inner_pipeline():
    global_task(path="./artifact.txt")


@task(script)
def global_task(path: Artifact[Path]):
    path.touch()

First of all, as you can see global_task is decorated with the @task instead of the @<pipeline-name>.task one. These tasks are not scoped to a single pipeline: every pipeline can import and use them. Their cache is also visible to all pipelines. In the example, one outer pipeline calls another pipeline and a global task equipped with an artifact. The node returned by a pipeline is special as it has access to all artifacts of its tasks. They can be accessed through the artifacts attribute by specifying both task and artifact name.

You can run:

sdag run outer_pipeline --local

to execute this example. When working with many nested pipelines, visualizations in the terminal quickly become crowded. You can use the --squeeze argument to collapse all inner pipelines into a unique node:

sdag view outer_pipeline --squeeze

Calling a task from another task is also easy. Copy the following snippet into the same module:

nested.py
@pipeline
def task_calling_task():
    outer_task()


@task_calling_task.task(script)
def outer_task():
    result = inner_task.fn(a=1)
    print(f"1 + 1 = {result}")


@task_calling_task.task(script)
def inner_task(a: int):
    return a + 1

Tasks have a fn attribute pointing to the decorated function. This reference can be used to directly call the function. Keep in mind that in this case inner_task does not spawn as a separate job. It is instead called as a normal function inside the outer_task process. You can run this example through:

sdag run task_calling_task --local

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: Overriding Configurations at Compile Time
docs.text:
When called inside a pipeline, tasks return their corresponding nodes in the graph. These nodes expose most configurations as attributes that can be modified at compile time to override their default values. Here is an example:

from sdag import ScriptPath, pipeline, script


@pipeline
def override():
    t = default_task()
    t.name = "custom_name"
    t.cache = "io"
    t.cache_size = 5
    t.script = ScriptPath(path="script.sh")
    t.cmd = "bash"

    t.envs["HELLO"] = "world"

    t.slurm.job_name = "default_job"
    t.slurm.account = "my-account"
    t.slurm.time = "00:00:30"
    t.slurm.output = "path/to/file.out"


@override.task(script)
def default_task(): ...

As you can see, it is possible to:

  • Modify properties like name, script, and caching behavior.
  • Define environment variables that are automatically set by the scheduler so you can access them during the task execution.
  • Override Slurm configurations set in the execution script. These are ignored if the task runs as a local bash process. When compared with those in pyproject.toml, hardcoded Slurm options have higher priority.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Tags can be used to specify custom configurations for groups of tasks. Tags can be added to tasks via the tags argument of the @taskor @<pipeline-name>.task decorator:

from sdag import script, task

@task(script, tags=["online", "small", "custom"])
def some_task(): ...

The corresponding configurations can be set either in the pyproject.toml under [[tool.sdag.tags]] or in the .sdag.toml file under [[tags]]:

pyproject.toml.sdag.toml 
[[tool.sdag.tags]]
tag = "online"
cmd = "bash"

[[tool.sdag.tags]]
tag = "small"
cpus-per-task = 1

[[tool.sdag.tags]]
tag = "custom"
script-path = "a/custom/script.sh"
envs = {"ENV_NAME" = "value"}

[[tags]]
tag = "online"
cmd = "bash"

[[tags]]
tag = "small"
cpus-per-task = 1

[[tags]]
tag = "custom"
script-path = "a/custom/script.sh"
envs = {"ENV_NAME" = "value"}

Tags have higher priority than pyproject.toml/.sdag.toml global configurations. Whenever a task is assigned more than one tag, such configurations are applied in the same order they are provided. Tags can be used to customize the behavior of groups of tasks. For example, some supercomputers have dedicated queues for jobs requiring internet access while others only allow outbound connections on login nodes. Tags can be used to enforce such policies. Moreover, tags specified in the .sdag.toml file override those in the pyproject.toml. So, different .sdag.toml files can be used to make pipelines run transparently across different machines without changing the source code. Tags currently allow one to customize:

  • cmd (bash or sbatch)
  • script-path: Used to change the execution script for selected tasks.
  • envs: Used to set additional environment variables
  • All Slurm settings available in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Unit Testing
docs.text:
Testing tasks is very easy. Decorated tasks have an fn attribute that holds a reference to the decorated function. This reference can be used to call tasks directly. You need to install pytest to run this example. Create a test/ folder inside the main project directory and add a test_tasks.py module inside it containing the following code:

test_tasks.py
from pathlib import Path

from sdag import Artifact, script, task


@task(script)
def task_with_input(a: int):
    return a + 1


@task(script)
def task_with_artifact(output_path: Artifact[Path]):
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    output_path.touch()


def test_task_output() -> None:
    assert task_with_input.fn(1) == 2


def test_artifact_exists(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    output_path = tmp_path / "artifact.txt"
    task_with_artifact.fn(output_path)
    assert output_path.is_file()

Simply run pytest to execute both tests and check they succeed.

docs.title: Caching and Artifacts
docs.text:
Caching is used to persist the output of a task across multiple runs, so you don't have to re-execute it again. Add the following pipeline to a new module in the main project directory:

caching.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def cached():
    t = cached_task(a="world")
    non_cached_task(t)


@cached.task(script, cache="io")
def cached_task(a: str):
    print(f"I only run once. The value of a is {a}")


@cached.task(script)
def non_cached_task():
    print("I run every time")

When this pipeline is executed the first time via:

sdag run cached --local

both tasks are scheduled. When executed again, cached_task will be cached, so it will be marked as completed without execution. For caching to be validated, all input values must match with the cached ones. You can try to modify the value of a to check the cache gets invalidated. You can increase the cache_size in the decorator (which is equal to 1 by default) to account for multiple values of a.

The cache is bound to a task name. Often, instead of increasing the cache size you can change the task name to provide it a whole new cache. Copy the following snippet into the same module:

caching.py
@pipeline
def name_change():
    a_task(value=1)
    t = a_task(value=2)
    t.name = "another_task"


@name_change.task(script, cache="io")
def a_task(value: int):
    print(f"value: {value}")

Because the two tasks have different names, they both get cached during the first execution, which can be triggered with:

sdag run name_change --local

You also get the extra benefit of showing the two tasks with different names in the logs.

docs.title: Artifacts
docs.text:
Artifacts can be used to signal to sdag that a task must produce some kind of output (typically files or folders). Copy the following snippet into the same module:

caching.py
from pathlib import Path

from sdag import Artifact


@pipeline
def dag_with_artifact():
    t = create_file(path="artifact.txt")
    print_path(input_path=t.artifacts["path"])


@dag_with_artifact.task(script, cache="io")
def create_file(path: Artifact[Path]):
    path.touch()


@dag_with_artifact.task(script, cache="io")
def print_path(input_path: str):
    print(f"The input path is {input_path}")

As you can see, Artifact[Path] is just a Path. You can also use Artifact[str] to leave the path as a string. During the first execution with:

sdag run dag_with_artifact --local

the artifact.txt file will be created in the main project directory. During successive execution the task will be marked as cached and not scheduled again. All artifacts must exist for a task to be marked as cached. This feature has been introduced so that if you accidentally delete the artifact or move it somewhere else, the task will be executed again to produce a new one in the correct path. You can try to delete artifact.txt and re-execute again the pipeline to verify the cache gets invalidated. Artifact paths can be passed around between tasks via their artifact attribute by specifying the task name. This is very useful when one task writes some data the next one must read.

You can use the describe command to visualize a bunch of useful information about the tasks of a pipeline including whether they are cached, their input values, and the artifact they are expected to produce. Running:

sdag describe dag_with_artifact

should print something like:

┌─────┬─────────────┬───────────────────┬────────┬───────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ uid │ name        │ pipeline          │ cached │ artifacts │ kwargs                         │
├─────┼─────────────┼───────────────────┼────────┼───────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
│     │             │                   │        │           │ {                              │
│   2 │ create_file │ dag_with_artifact │ true   │ path      │   "path": "artifact.txt"       │
│     │             │                   │        │           │ }                              │
├─────┼─────────────┼───────────────────┼────────┼───────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
│     │             │                   │        │           │ {                              │
│   3 │ print_path  │ dag_with_artifact │ true   │           │   "input_path": "artifact.txt" │
│     │             │                   │        │           │ }                              │
└─────┴─────────────┴───────────────────┴────────┴───────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

sdag prune can be used to prune the cache of tasks or pipelines. Run:

sdag prune create_file -p dag_with_artifact

to delete the cache of the create_file task. Check out the CLI section for details.

docs.title: Caching options
docs.text:
Several caching options are available:

Cache option Cache validation conditions "none" Disables caching (default value). "output" Artifacts exist. "io" Artifacts exist and input values match. Values allowed to change can be listed under cache_ignore. "task" Same as "io" but the task function code must also match. "project" Same as "io" but the code of all internal modules imported during the pipeline compilation must also match.

docs.title: Cache locking
docs.text:
By default, a cached task lock is enabled. Consider the following pipeline:

cache_lock.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def cache_lock():
    """Simple example to test cache locking.

    This pipeline shows how cache locking works.
    Only two tasks will run here, one with a=1
    and the other a=2. The other ones will wait
    and then get cached.
    """
    lock_cache(a=1)
    lock_cache(a=1)
    lock_cache(a=1)
    lock_cache(a=1)
    lock_cache(a=2)
    lock_cache(a=2)


@cache_lock.task(script, cache="io", cache_size=2)
def lock_cache(a: int) -> None:
    """Wait without doing much.

    Args:
        a (int): input value.
    """
    import time

    print(a)
    time.sleep(7)

If you execute it through the command:

sdag run cache_lock --local

You will see that only two tasks will be actually executed, the other ones will wait and then get cached after the successful completion of the running tasks. To be matching, two conditions must hold:

  1. The tasks must share the same cache, which means they must have the same name and scope. The scope of a task can be local to a pipeline like lock_cache in the example or global as shown in the Nested Calls section.
  2. Their inputs are equal, ignoring any values listed in cache_ignore. This condition doesn't apply when cache="output".

The example sets cache_size=2 so that the results for a=1 and a=2 both fit in the cache. You can turn off this feature by disabling the cache-lock flag in the pyproject.toml configurations.

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
The pipeline structure can be dynamically altered based on the output of other tasks. Add the following pipeline to a new module in the main project directory:

control_flow.py
from sdag import Elif, Else, If, pipeline, script


@pipeline
def control_flow():
    with If(condition1()):
        option1()
    with Elif(condition2()):
        option2()
    with Else():
        option3()


@control_flow.task(script)
def condition1() -> bool:
    return False


@control_flow.task(script)
def condition2() -> bool:
    return True


@control_flow.task(script)
def option1():
    print("Option 1 selected")


@control_flow.task(script)
def option2():
    print("Option 2 selected")


@control_flow.task(script)
def option3():
    print("Option 3 selected")

condition1 and condition2 are tasks that must return a Boolean value. Run:

sdag run control_flow --local

to execute the example. The expected flow is:

  1. condition1 is executed and returns False.
  2. Because the output is False, option1 is skipped and condition2 is evaluated.
  3. The output of condition2 is True, so option2 is executed while option3 is skipped.

docs.title: OneOf
docs.text:
One might expect the following snippet to work as expected:

@pipeline
def dag():
    with If(condition1()):
        t = option1()
    with Else():
        t = option2()
    final_task(t)

Unfortunately, it's not! t in the example will always refer to option2. The oneof node is inspired by Kubeflow and it can be used to reference tasks running on separate branches. Add the following snippet to the same control_flow.py module:

control_flow.py
from sdag import oneof


@pipeline
def oneof_example():
    with If(condition()):
        t1 = first_alternative()
    with Else():
        t2 = second_alternative()
    t = oneof(t1, t2)
    final_task(t)


@oneof_example.task(script)
def condition() -> bool:
    return False


@oneof_example.task(script)
def first_alternative():
    print("alternative 1 selected")


@oneof_example.task(script)
def second_alternative():
    print("alternative 2 selected")


@oneof_example.task(script)
def final_task():
    print("final task")

Here, final_task will only run if at least one between first_alternative and second_alternative executes successfully. You can run the example through:

sdag run oneof_example --local

You can also use oneof when multiple concurrent tasks are executed. It will become the first task of the pool that completes the execution without errors.

@pipeline
def dag():
    t_fail = will_fail()
    t_slow = slow_task()
    t_fast = fast_task()

    # Likely equal to t_fast
    first_to_complete = oneof(t_fail, t_slow, t_fast)

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: External tasks
docs.text:
Tasks are often just regular Python functions wrapped by sdag. However, you might also want to run Bash scripts, executables, or perhaps a piece of code unrelated to the sdag project. Tasks can be marked as external to inform sdag they do not wrap a Python function. Copy the following pipeline into a new module in the main project directory:

external_local_tasks.py
from sdag import Script, pipeline


@pipeline
def external_dag():
    external_task(input_data="world")


@external_dag.task(Script("echo $INPUT_DATA"), mode="ext")
def external_task(input_data: str): ...

You can either write a separate bash script and insert its path into the decorator or use the Script object to embed its content into the module. Here, the Python function is only used to define the graph node and it's not actually called by the scheduler. Uppercased input values are set as environment variables by sdag, so you can use them inside the external script. You can run this example through:

sdag run external_dag --local

Warning

Input arguments like path or user might cause troubles as they would override the corresponding PATH and USER environment variables. For this reason, a compile-time error is thrown when the input variables of external tasks might override POSIX environment variables. The obvious solution is to use safer names like input_path instead of path.

docs.title: Local tasks
docs.text:
Unlike other libraries, in sdag you don't specify a runner for the whole pipeline. Local and Slurm tasks can be freely mixed in the same workflow. This choice has been made to avoid spinning Slurm jobs that may stay in queue forever just to perform small operations that could be easily executed locally. Add a new pipeline to external_local_tasks.py:

external_local_tasks.py
from sdag import script


@pipeline
def local_dag():
    local_task()


@local_dag.task(script, cmd="bash")
def local_task():
    print("I run locally!")

cmd="bash" is used to specify that the task must run as a nonblocking, local process instead of a Slurm job. This pipeline can now be executed with:

sdag run local_dag

Under the hood, the --local option used in many other examples simply sets cmd="bash" to all tasks, thus forcing them to run as local processes.

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: Failure Recovery
docs.text:
Failures are unfortunately very common in HPC. In the context of sdag, the two most common failures that can happen are:

  1. The sdag scheduler gets killed
  2. Tasks fail for whatever reason

docs.title: Scheduler failures
docs.text:
The scheduler checkpoints its status. So, in case of failures it can be restarted from where it left off. To restart the scheduler, run:

sdag restart <pipeline-name>

Once restarted, it gets from Slurm the status of the supposedly running jobs to update the graph state. However, all previously running local jobs (that get killed if the scheduler goes down) are marked as failed.

docs.title: Task failures
docs.text:
Add the following pipeline to a new module in the main project directory:

failure_recovery.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def failure():
    t = failed_task()
    will_never_run(t)


@failure.task(script)
def failed_task():
    raise ValueError("Failing...")


@failure.task(script)
def will_never_run():
    print("You will never see this message")

Run:

sdag run failure --local

to execute the pipeline. As expected, failed_task fails and all dependent nodes are skipped. If you fix the bug and the graph structure doesn't change, you can retry the run and see if it completes successfully:

sdag retry failure

retry will reset all failed and skipped tasks before continuing the run. If no tasks failed or get skipped, then sdag retry is virtually identical to the sdag restart command of the previous section. You can also set the number of retries for a task. Modify failed_task as follows:

@failure.task(script, retries=2)
def failed_task():
    raise ValueError("Failing...")

And run the pipeline again:

sdag run failure --local

You will see that the execution of failed_task is retried two times before marking it as failed definitively.

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: Hello World in sdag
docs.text:
After installing sdag, copy the following code into a module named hello.py in the main project directory:

hello.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def hello_world():
    say_hello(name="sdag")


@hello_world.task(script)
def say_hello(name: str):
    print(f"hello from {name}")

There are two main objects in sdag, pipelines and tasks. Pipelines (marked with the @pipeline decorator) are used to represent the structure of the graph that will be executed. Tasks (marked with @task or <pipeline-name>@task decorators) are jobs scheduled depending on the current state of the graph. The script argument of the task decorator contains the script fired by the scheduler. This pipeline can be compiled with:

sdag compile hello:hello_world --local

Where hello:hello_world is the pipeline import string in the form path.to.module:function. The previous command generates a hello_world.json file, which is saved in a ./compiled-pipelines folder created by sdag. In many cases, you won't have to specify the full import string as sdag is able to discover pipelines simply by their name:

sdag compile hello_world --local

Info

In more structured codebases it is convenient to explicitly define the base directory pipelines are searched into. Check out the Structuring Larger Projects for details.

To run the compiled pipeline, execute:

sdag run hello_world.json

This command will start the scheduler and execute the say_hello task. You should see tables like this one printed in the terminal (the task PID will likely be different):

    ┌─────┬───────────┬─────────────┬───────────────────────┬──────┬─────────┐
    │ uid │ task      │ pipeline    │ status                │ cmd  │ try_num │
    ├─────┼───────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────┼──────┼─────────┤
    │   2 │ say_hello │ hello_world │ Running (pid=3085406) │ bash │ 1       │
    └─────┴───────────┴─────────────┴───────────────────────┴──────┴─────────┘

If you instead executed:

sdag run hello_world --local

(thus without pointing to a compiled JSON file), the hello_world pipeline would be compiled on-the-fly and then immediately executed. Some sdag commands accept either pipeline names, import strings, or compiled JSON paths. The latter allows one to skip the compilation step. You can check out the CLI section for additional information.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: To correctly monitor jobs, sdag requires the --json option to be available both to squeue and sacct.

docs.title: Running on Slurm
docs.text:
Let's consider the pipeline of the previous Section:

hello.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def hello_world():
    say_hello(name="sdag")


@hello_world.task(script)
def say_hello(name: str):
    print(f"hello from {name}")

So far, the --local option is used to run tasks locally. There are several ways to run them on Slurm instead.

Custom scriptsGlobal configurationsNode override

Create a submit.sh sbatch script in the main project directory and paste the following content:

submit.sh
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=<account-name>
#SBATCH --partition=<partition-name>
#SBATCH --qos=<qos-name>
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --tasks-per-node=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --time=00:00:30

sdag-execute

Now, add the script path to the task decorator:

hello.py
@hello_world.task("submit.sh")
def say_hello(name: str):
    print(f"hello from {name}")

Bringing custom sbatch scripts is a very flexible approach for jobs that require some preparation before execution (like spinning up a Ray cluster) and for external tasks.

Add the following configurations to your pyproject.toml file:

pyproject.toml
[tool.sdag]
account="<account-name>"
partition="<partition-name>"
qos="<qos-name>"
nodes=1
cpus-per-task=1
time="00:02:00"

These configurations are applied globally to all tasks. Check out the Configuration section for details and the Tags section for configuring groups of tasks.

Modify the pipeline as follows:

hello.py
@pipeline
def hello_world():
    t = say_hello(name="sdag")
    t.slurm.account = <account-name>
    t.slurm.partition = <partition-name>
    t.slurm.qos = <qos-name>
    t.slurm.nodes = 1
    t.slurm.tasks_per_node = 1
    t.slurm.cpus_per_task = 1
    t.slurm.time = "00:00:30"

This approach works best for fine tuning some configurations for specific nodes. Check out the Override section for details.

Info

job-name, output, and error are intentionally missing here as sdag overrides them by default.

<account-name>, <partition-name>, and <qos-name> in the examples are the Slurm account, partition, and quality of service you have access to. These approaches can also be used in combination with each other: The account name can be set at the project level, custom scripts are used to prepare the execution of specific jobs and single nodes might override their own wall time. When in conflict, the priority is: node overrides > global settings > sbatch scripts.

Now that the configurations are set, the pipeline can be run on Slurm via:

sdag run hello_world

By default, task logs are written in a logs/ folder created in the main project directory.

docs.title: Input and Output Data
docs.text:
Keyword arguments can be used to take as input the output of a previous task. Copy the following pipeline into a new module:

input_and_output.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def output_use():
    t = return_output()
    take_input(world=t)


@output_use.task(script)
def return_output():
    return "world"


@output_use.task(script)
def take_input(world: str):
    print(f"Hello, {world}!")

sdag view output_use will print:

   ╭──────╮
   │_root_│
   ╰──────╯
       │
       │
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│return_output│
└─────────────┘
       │
       │
       │output
       ▼
 ┌──────────┐
 │take_input│
 └──────────┘

So, the output of return_output is used as input in the take_input task.

Warning

Output data is serialized as JSON under the hood, which means only JSON-serializable objects are allowed (e.g., lists are fine but tuples are not). Because we don't want to enforce default serialization methods, when working with complex or large data structures it is recommended to serialize them separately and move their paths around as artifacts.

You can run the example via:

sdag run output_use --local

Pipelines can take input arguments as well. Add the following code to the same module:

input_and_output.py
from pathlib import Path


@pipeline
def dag_with_input(input_path):
    use_input_path(input_path=input_path)


@dag_with_input.task(script)
def use_input_path(input_path: Path):
    print(f"Input path: '{input_path}'; type: {type(input_path)}")

Input argument can be passed to the pipeline as extra CLI arguments:

sdag run dag_with_input --local --input-path=a/path

You can use -- to make sure extra arguments are not overshadowed by the sdag CLI:

sdag run dag_with_input --local -- --input-path=a/path

It is also possible to run a specific task of a pipeline via sdag runtask. One must specify task, pipeline it belongs to, and pass all input arguments as extra CLI args:

sdag runtask use_input_path dag_with_input --local --input-path=a/path

Notice that input_path is automatically cast to Path. We only do this with paths to eliminate a frequent pattern showing up in our pipelines:

@dag_with_input.task(script)
def use_input_path(input1: str, input2: str):
    input1_path = Path(input1)
    input2_path = Path(input2)
    ...

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: Handling Multiple Tasks
docs.text:
Copy the following pipeline into a new module in the main project directory:

multiple_tasks.py
from sdag import pipeline, script


@pipeline
def many_tasks():
    say_hello()
    say_hello()
    say_hello()


@many_tasks.task(script)
def say_hello():
    print("hello world!")

You can view the graph of this pipeline in the terminal via sdag view:

sdag view many_tasks

which should print something like:

                    ╭──────╮
                    │_root_│
                    ╰──────╯
                        │
                        │
     ┌──────────────────└──────────────────┐
     ▼                  ▼                  ▼
┌─────────┐        ┌─────────┐        ┌─────────┐
│say_hello│        │say_hello│        │say_hello│
└─────────┘        └─────────┘        └─────────┘

As these tasks do not depend on each other, they are scheduled at the same time. You can confirm this by running the pipeline:

sdag run many_tasks --local

You can use positional arguments to signal graph edges. Let's add a second pipeline to the same many_tasks.py module:

multiple_tasks.py
import asyncio

@pipeline
def dependent_tasks():
    t1 = first()
    t2 = first()
    second(t1, t2)


@dependent_tasks.task(script)
def first():
    print("I run first!")


@dependent_tasks.task(script)
async def second():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    print("I run second!")

Notice async tasks are supported: in such cases sdag will start the event loop for you. sdag view dependent_tasks will now print:

       ╭──────╮
       │_root_│
       ╰──────╯
           │
           │
   ┌───────└──────┐
   ▼              ▼
┌─────┐        ┌─────┐
│first│        │first│
└─────┘        └─────┘
   │              │
   │              │
   └───────┌──────┘
           ▼
       ┌──────┐
       │second│
       └──────┘

Which means that second will only run if both first tasks successfully complete. This example can be run via:

sdag run dependent_tasks --local

Info

Check out the Slurm section to run this example on Slurm.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
As shown in the previous sections, you can use sdag view <pipeline-name> to visualize graphs in the terminal. However, when graphs become large this visualization quickly becomes messy and hard to understand. For this reason, sdag provides another quick visualization method. To leverage it, you must install the neo4j-viz library.

To visualize the dependent_tasks pipeline of the Handling multiple tasks section, copy the following snippet into a Jupyter notebook cell:

from sdag import DAGViewer


viewer = DAGViewer()
viewer.view("dependent_tasks")

You should see the graph of the pipeline printed in the cell. You can change the attributes of DAGViewer to modify colors and sizes of the graph nodes.
